front.title: Post-Session Execution Assurance (PSEA): A Wire Protocol for Verifying Authority at the Moment of Action

abstract.t: Session-based authentication establishes identity at login but does not preserve evidence of human authorization at the moment a specific action is executed. Post-Session Execution Assurance (PSEA) is a security model that requires cryptographic proof of human presence, device integrity, and execution authority at the moment of action, independent of prior session state. This document specifies the PSEA wire protocol -- canonical encoding, proof token formats, four enforcement tiers (Passive, Silent, Explicit, Authoritative), trust state systems, verifier endpoints, error code registry, and security considerations -- for Informational status via the Independent Submission Stream.

section.name: Introduction
section.t: This document specifies Post-Session Execution Assurance (PSEA), a wire protocol for verifying human authority at the moment a sensitive action is executed. PSEA does not replace authentication; it requires cryptographic proof of authority at the moment of execution, independent of prior session state.

section.name: The Authority Gap
section.t: For decades, session-based security has operated on the assumption that a successful authentication event at login time represents the user's identity and authority for the duration of the session. In modern systems, where actions occur long after the initial authentication event and context drifts continuously, this assumption is no longer reasonable: a session authenticated by a legitimate user at 09:00 carries identical authority at 15:00, even if the device has been compromised, the user has stepped away, or an automated process has assumed control of the session. Authentication answers "Did this entity present valid credentials at some point in time?"; execution authority answers "Is an authorized human, present, verified, and operating from a trusted device, approving this specific action right now?". The gap between these two questions is where risk materializes, and it is the problem PSEA addresses.

Concretely: a banking session authenticated at 09:00 is still "valid" at 15:00 when a high-value fund transfer is submitted -- yet session validity says nothing about whether the legitimate account holder, present and aware, actually approved that transfer at that moment, as opposed to a hijacked session, malware acting autonomously, or an unattended unlocked device. The same gap recurs wherever a high-consequence action rides on a still-open session: dispensing a controlled drug, recording a safety-critical shift check-in, or escalating an administrator's privileges. Session-valid is not the same property as this specific human approved this specific action, right now. PSEA's purpose is to produce cryptographic Evidence of the latter at execution time, independent of session state.

section.name: Document Scope and Status
section.t: This document is Informational and is submitted through the Independent Submission Stream . It defines the PSEA wire protocol: canonical encoding, proof token formats, the four enforcement tiers, trust state systems, verifier endpoints, error response codes, and accompanying security considerations. The wire formats and rules described in this document are sufficient on their own to build a conforming implementation; a reference implementation exists informatively but is not a normative dependency.

section.name: Applicability
section.t: PSEA is applicable to any deployment that needs an after-the-fact cryptographic record showing that a human user was present at a specific device at a specific moment and approved a specific action. The wire protocol is domain-neutral; this document does not enumerate or endorse particular industries or regulatory regimes, and does not claim compliance with any external compliance framework. Deployers are responsible for any compliance mapping they choose to claim against their own regulatory environment.

section.name: PSEA Architecture
section.t: This section borrows the vocabulary of Remote ATtestation procedureS (RATS) for conceptual alignment with the IETF security community. The terminology is used informatively only: PSEA is NOT a RATS profile and does not claim format-level RATS or CWT conformance. The Tier E / Tier A proof reuses a subset of Entity Attestation Token claims () -- ueid, eat_nonce, and submods -- inside a JWS/JWT for device-state conveyance (), but PSEA does not claim full EAT conformance. The role mapping below is a descriptive analogy; the normative wire shape is defined in Sections 3 through 8 of this document.

section.name: The Passport Model in PSEA
section.t: PSEA's data flow resembles the passport model described in , Section 5.1: the Attester transmits Evidence to the Verifier; the Verifier appraises the Evidence and produces an Attestation Result that the Relying Party consumes. This resemblance is informative; the normative wire shape is in Sections 4 and 7, not derived from RATS.

The Attester MAY relay the Attestation Result on behalf of the Relying Party (for example, a mobile trust-anchor device that delivers the Attestation Result to the application server it is acting on behalf of), but the appraisal authority remains with the Verifier. The background- check model defined in , Section 5.2 is not used by PSEA and SHOULD NOT be assumed by implementations.

section.name: Co-location of Verifier and Relying Party
section.t: A PSEA implementation MAY co-locate the Verifier and the Relying Party in a single deployment (the Relying Party's backend both appraises Evidence and gates the action). It MAY also separate them (the Verifier is operated as an independent service whose Attestation Results are consumed by multiple Relying Parties).

The Verifier MUST produce Attestation Results that are cryptographically integrity- protected so that a non-co-located Relying Party can verify their authenticity independently. The wire format of the Attestation Result is defined in .

section.name: Subject Distinction
section.t: The trust-anchor device is the sole Attester in a PSEA deployment. Natural persons are not Attesters, in the sense of , Section 3.1: the Attester role is restricted to computational devices capable of generating Evidence. The human is the subject of the Evidence the Attester produces. states the normative requirement that the Attester's Evidence include a cryptographic binding to a user-verification event at the moment (or, for Tier S, at the bootstrap) of the action being attested.

section.name: Architectural Principles
section.t: The following five principles are normative for PSEA-conformant deployments. They map directly to the wire-protocol requirements in , , and .

section.name: Execution-Time Proof
section.t: Evidence MUST be generated at the moment a sensitive action is approved, not in advance and not in arrears. Pre-generated or session-cached evidence does not satisfy this requirement (Tier S is the explicit exception, in which the bootstrap evidence is generated at session start and the session-cached maintenance evidence is permitted within bounded conditions; see ).

section.name: Human Presence Assurance
section.t: A PSEA-conformant tier that approves a specific action with execution-time human authorization (Tier E and Tier A; see ) MUST include, in the proof of approval, Evidence that a human user was actively present at the trust-anchor device at the moment of approval. The presence Evidence MUST be cryptographically bound to the signing operation that produced the approval.

A PSEA-conformant tier that produces background attestation without human action approval (Tier P; see ) does not require human-presence Evidence. The guarantee Tier P provides is defined in and does not include execution-time human authorization.

In all cases where presence Evidence is required, presence MUST be demonstrated, not assumed. Presence Evidence is distinct from identity recall, in which a system infers human presence from a prior authentication event such as login.

The trust-anchor device is the Attester and the human user is the subject of the Evidence the Attester produces. The human is not a separate Attester. PSEA proves that a human was present and approved this specific action; it does NOT identify which human — identity attribution is the deployment's responsibility and is out of scope of this specification. The mechanism by which the trust-anchor device verifies human presence is equally out of scope. Examples of valid mechanisms include (but are not limited to): a platform biometric subsystem (face or fingerprint match), a hardware token PIN entry, a magnetic-stripe card swipe combined with a PIN, a smartcard with PIN, a WebAuthn-style authenticator with user verification, or any other platform-provided user-verification primitive. The normative requirement is that some contemporaneous user-verification event gated the signing operation; PSEA is mechanism-agnostic about which.

section.name: Device-Bound Trust
section.t: Trust is anchored in the specific physical device that performed the user-verification event. The Attester's signing key MUST be hardware-bound (for example, in a Trusted Execution Environment, Secure Enclave, StrongBox, or equivalent), MUST NOT be extractable from the device, and MUST be invalidated by the platform on revocation events (factory reset, re-enrollment of the platform user-verification credential set if the implementation binds the key to that set, etc.). Cross-device transferable signing material does not satisfy this requirement.

section.name: Cryptographic Proof
section.t: Trust is established through cryptographic mechanisms, not inferred from session tokens, cookies, or bearer credentials. The Evidence MUST be independently verifiable and resistant to replay, forgery, and delegation.

All four PSEA tiers and the Verifier acknowledgement are carried as JWS Compact Serialization (): the Tier E / Tier A proof, the Tier P PToken, the Tier S SessionSummary, and the Tier E / Tier A acknowledgement are each a compact JWS whose signature covers the received BASE64URL(header) || "." || BASE64URL(payload) octets, so peer verification is over the bytes on the wire and does not depend on re-canonicalization of the claim set. Canonical encoding per -- a simplified subset of the JSON Canonicalization Scheme () -- remains load-bearing for exactly one place where a hash is taken over canonical JSON octets: the action-payload binding (the SHA-256 over the canonical actionPayload that the Verifier re-computes and compares against the signed psea_payload_hash claim; ). The simplification -- integer-only numeric serialization -- is documented in ; an implementation that requires full conformance produces output identical to for that action-payload hash.

section.name: Connectivity Independence
section.t: A PSEA-conformant tier MAY require Verifier reachability for action approval, or MAY operate with deferred Verifier interaction, depending on the tier's security model.

Tiers P, S, and E (see ) MUST be capable of generating Evidence offline; Verifier-side appraisal MAY be deferred. Tier A () requires synchronous Verifier authorization and MUST NOT proceed without Verifier reachability; the Attester MUST surface OFFLINE_AUTHORITATIVE_BLOCKED () when the Verifier is unreachable.

In all cases, Evidence MUST be generated at the moment of action approval, not in advance and not in arrears. Deferred verification MUST NOT permit admission of stale Evidence or Evidence whose cryptographic binding to the action being approved cannot be established.

section.name: What PSEA Is Not
section.t: Clarity about the boundaries of PSEA is essential to prevent conflation with existing security paradigms.

PSEA is not Multi-Factor Authentication. MFA strengthens the login boundary by requiring multiple credential types. It does not address authority at execution time. Once MFA is completed, the resulting session carries the same inherited trust as any other session.

PSEA is not Continuous Authentication. Continuous authentication monitors behavioral or other signals throughout a session to detect anomalies. It is a monitoring and risk-scoring mechanism. It does not require Evidence of authority at the moment of a specific action.

PSEA is not Session Hardening. Session hardening techniques such as those described in -- short timeouts, token rotation, binding to IP addresses -- reduce the window of exposure. They do not verify who is executing an action within that window.

PSEA is not Risk-Based Authentication. Risk-based systems evaluate contextual signals to adjust authentication requirements dynamically. They operate at or near the login boundary. They do not provide execution-time Evidence.

PSEA is not a rebranding of Zero Trust. Zero Trust architectures reduce implicit trust between system components and enforce verification at network and application boundaries. PSEA addresses a different problem: the absence of verified authority at the point of action execution, which persists even within Zero Trust environments.

section.name: Relationship to WebAuthn and FIDO Transaction Confirmation
section.t: WebAuthn and FIDO2 provide phishing-resistant, hardware-backed authentication and are the strongest widely deployed primitives for the login boundary. A natural question is whether their transaction-confirmation features already solve the execution-time authority problem PSEA targets. As a matter of deployment reality, they do not.

Web Authentication Level 1 defined two transaction-confirmation extensions: txAuthSimple (display a text prompt and bind the user's approval of that exact text into the signed assertion) and txAuthGeneric (the same for a hashed content blob). These were the mechanism by which a WebAuthn assertion could attest that the user approved a specific transaction -- a What-You-See-Is-What-You-Sign (WYSIWYS) binding. No browser implemented these extensions, and they were removed in Web Authentication Level 2. A current WebAuthn assertion therefore attests that an authenticator holding a given credential was exercised with user presence (and optionally user verification), but it does not cryptographically bind the assertion to a specific application-level action or to human-readable transaction content.

Consequently, the transaction-binding / WYSIWYS property -- proof that a present, verified human approved a specific named action, with specific content, at the moment of execution -- is not provided by any deployed authentication standard today. PSEA addresses precisely this gap: a PSEA proof binds the action identity and a SHA-256 hash of the action payload (the fail-closed action-binding defined later in this document) into a hardware-signed Attestation produced at execution time. PSEA is complementary to WebAuthn and FIDO rather than a replacement: WebAuthn and FIDO2 remain appropriate for establishing the session and verifying the human's credential, while PSEA supplies the per-action execution-time Evidence that the transaction-confirmation extensions were intended to provide but, in deployed form, do not.

section.name: Relationship to OAuth 2.0 Step-Up Authentication
section.t: OAuth 2.0 Step-Up Authentication Challenge defines a mechanism by which an OAuth-protected resource server signals to a client that the bearer access token presented does not satisfy the resource's authentication requirements. The resource server responds with HTTP 401 and a WWW-Authenticate challenge carrying a required Authentication Context Class Reference (acr_values) and/or a maximum authentication age (max_age). The client then drives the user through re-authentication and obtains a new access token that satisfies the requirement.

RFC 9470 and PSEA address adjacent but distinct points in the access-control chain. Both react to the same operational gap: an access token or session that was sufficient at issuance time may be insufficient at the moment a higher-risk action is requested. They differ in the unit of escalation and in the cryptographic properties of the artifact produced.

section.name: Complementarity
section.t: RFC 9470 step-up and PSEA MAY be composed: the first to signal that a per-action authority check is required; the second to produce the cryptographically action-bound Evidence that satisfies that check.

ol.li: An OAuth-protected resource server, acting as a Relying Party (), receives a request whose access token does not satisfy the resource's per-action policy.
The resource server returns HTTP 401 with a WWW-Authenticate challenge per , indicating the required step-up.

The client drives the step-up flow on a device hosting a PSEA trust-anchor (). The trust-anchor device produces fresh Evidence at the tier the resource's policy demands (), cryptographically bound to the specific action that triggered the 401.

The client re-submits the request, conveying the Evidence to the Verifier. The Verifier appraises the Evidence and produces an Attestation Result. The resource server gates the action on both the OAuth access token (session validity) and the Attestation Result (per-action authority).

section.t: In this composition, OAuth supplies the session and identity context; PSEA supplies the per- action cryptographic authority proof. Neither mechanism replaces the other.

section.name: Out of Scope for This Document
section.t: This section identifies architectural complementarity. It does not define a normative integration profile between PSEA and . A normative integration profile (specifying the precise WWW-Authenticate challenge syntax, the acr_values registration for PSEA tiers, the error-mapping table between RFC 9470 challenges and PSEA error codes, and the conveyance of the Evidence in the re-submitted request) is deferred to a future document.

section.name: Canonical Encoding of Proof Payloads
section.t: The canonical encoding rules in this section apply wherever a PSEA hash is taken over canonical JSON octets. All four PSEA tiers and the Verifier acknowledgement are now carried as JWS Compact Serialization (), whose signatures cover the received wire octets directly; canonical encoding is therefore not load-bearing for verifying any of those JWS objects. It remains MUST-strength for exactly one use, in which the producer and the Verifier independently hash canonical JSON bytes with SHA-256 and compare the result:

ul.li: the action-payload binding -- the SHA-256 over the canonical actionPayload that produces the signed psea_payload_hash claim, which the Verifier independently re-computes and compares ().

section.t: For this use, implementations that deviate from the rules below will produce byte sequences that fail the payload-binding comparison on peer platforms.

The canonical encoding defined here is a simplified subset of the JSON Canonicalization Scheme (JCS) specified in . Implementers MUST read this section in full before relying on a JSON library's default serialization or a third-party JCS implementation; platform defaults frequently diverge from these requirements in ways that are difficult to detect without cross-platform test vectors.
This document uses the verb "will" in lowercase to describe deterministic consequences of non-conformance, not as a BCP 14 keyword.

section.name: UTF-8 Serialization
section.t: The canonical byte sequence MUST be encoded as UTF-8 . The encoding MUST NOT include a byte-order mark.

section.name: Object Key Ordering (Case-Sensitive Unicode Code-Point Sort)
section.t: Object members MUST be ordered by case-sensitive ascending Unicode code-point comparison of their keys, byte by byte after UTF-8 encoding. The comparison MUST NOT normalize case, fold Unicode equivalence classes, or apply collation rules. Two keys that differ only in case (for example, "endedAt" and "endReason") MUST order according to the Unicode code-point value of their differing character; in this example, "endReason" (uppercase "R" = U+0052 = 82) sorts before "endedAt" (lowercase "e" at the comparison position = U+0065 = 101) because 82 < 101.
This rule is the canonical encoding's most consequential implementer-warning point. See for cross-platform notes.

section.name: Array Ordering
section.t: JSON arrays preserve their natural element order; the canonical encoding MUST NOT re-order array elements. The semantics of array order are payload-specific and are defined where applicable in .

section.name: String Serialization
section.t: String values MUST be serialized following the encoding rules in , Section 3.2.2.2 (Serialization of Strings). In particular: the JSON six- character escape forms for U+0022 (quotation mark), U+005C (reverse solidus), U+0008, U+000C, U+000A, U+000D, and U+0009 MUST be used; the "\uXXXX" form MUST use lowercase hexadecimal digits; surrogate pairs MUST be emitted as written by the producer (canonical encoding does not normalize Unicode form).

section.name: Number Serialization (Simplified Subset)
section.t: PSEA payload schemas define numeric fields only as integers. The canonical encoding of an integer N MUST be the shortest non-negative decimal representation (no leading zeros, no "+" sign, no exponent, no decimal point). The integer-only subset is the simplification this document takes from ; an implementation that requires full RFC 8785 conformance produces output identical to the rule in this subsection for all payload schemas defined in this revision.

Floating-point numbers, decimal fractions, and exponent notation MUST NOT appear in any PSEA payload field at this revision. A future revision MAY extend the subset; until such an extension is registered, any non-integer numeric value in a signed payload field is non-conformant.

section.name: Boolean and Null Serialization
section.t: The literals true, false, and null MUST be serialized with their lowercase JSON spelling. null as a value SHOULD NOT appear in PSEA payload schemas; absent fields are conveyed by omitting the key rather than by including the key with a null value.

section.name: Whitespace
section.t: The canonical encoding MUST NOT include whitespace between tokens (no spaces, tabs, newlines, or carriage returns). Whitespace inside string values is preserved verbatim per .

section.name: Conformance and Cross-Platform Implementer Warning
section.t: Implementations MUST verify their canonical encoder against the test vectors in . A canonical encoder that produces output matching the test vectors for every input in that appendix is conformant; an encoder that diverges on any single test vector is non-conformant and will produce signed bytes that fail peer verification.
Specific implementer-warning notes on common platform pitfalls:

dl.dd: JSONSerialization with the sortedKeys option performs a case-INSENSITIVE sort, which diverges from this section's case-SENSITIVE rule (see ). Implementations on Apple platforms MUST NOT rely on sortedKeys; they MUST emit canonical bytes via a manual sort using a case-sensitive comparator (for example, Swift's Dictionary.keys.sorted() with the default less-than operator on String, which is case-sensitive).

Array.prototype.sort() on string keys performs a case-sensitive Unicode code-point sort, matching this section's requirement. JSON.stringify with a comparator option is not standard; use a manual canonicalization pass.

String.compareTo() performs case-sensitive Unicode code-point comparison; the standard JCS implementations in major libraries (Jackson, Gson) produce conformant output when configured for canonical mode.
The standard sorted() on strings performs case-sensitive Unicode code-point sort. The json module's sort_keys=True matches this section's rule.
Default string comparison on both languages is case-sensitive byte-wise on UTF-8, which matches this section's rule for keys composed entirely of ASCII characters.

section.t: The most common bug surfaced by the 2026-05-18 cross-platform verification effort was an Apple sortedKeys case-insensitive sort silently producing canonical bytes that diverged from the backend (which used JavaScript's case-sensitive default sort) -- causing every iOS-signed session batch to fail signature verification. This is the failure mode the implementer-warning here is specifically designed to prevent.

section.name: Proof Token Format
section.t: A Tier E or Tier A PSEA proof is a JWS Compact Serialization object (): BASE64URL(protected header) || "." || BASE64URL(payload) || "." || BASE64URL(signature). The Attester signs the header.payload octets with its hardware-bound key. The claim set reuses JWT registered claims (), a subset of Entity Attestation Token claims () for device-state conveyance, and PSEA-private psea_* claims. The proof travels in a transport body () alongside the unsigned cleartext actionPayload that the Verifier independently hashes and compares against the signed payload-hash claim.

The integrity flows are: the proof's authenticity and integrity are established by the JWS signature over its received octets; the action binding is established by the Verifier re-hashing the cleartext actionPayload and comparing to the signed psea_payload_hash claim (); the AttestationBlock carried in integrityEvidence is appraised independently against the platform Endorsement; and chainEntry is computed deterministically by the Verifier from signed inputs, so its integrity flows from the signature on those inputs.

Tier P (PToken, ) and Tier S (SessionSummary, ) are also JWS Compact Serialization objects, distinguished from the Tier E / Tier A proof only by their protected-header typ value, their kid derivation, and their claim set, as specified in their respective sections. All four tiers share one uniform compact-JWS wire format.

section.t: The receiving endpoint determines which psea_tier value the Verifier expects in the payload: /verify () carries Tier E proofs (psea_tier == "E"); /authorize carries Tier A proofs (psea_tier == "A"). The payload's psea_tier, aud, and iss claims together close the cross-replay attack surface (Section 4.9.5).
The transport body POSTed to the endpoint wraps the JWS in the proof field and carries the cleartext action and evidence alongside it:

The actionPayload is unsigned cleartext; the Verifier re-canonicalizes it (), takes its SHA-256, and compares the result against the signed psea_payload_hash claim. This comparison is the fail-closed action binding (). Because a compact JWS has a single authoritative payload, the proof carries no envelope-level duplicates of the signed claims.

Tier P proofs and Tier S proofs use the same compact-JWS representation with distinct protected-header typ values, distinct claim sets, and distinct endpoints; see (PToken, /trustAttest) and (SessionSummary, /sessionBatch) respectively.

section.name: Single Authoritative Payload (No Envelope Duplicates)
section.t: A compact JWS has a single, cryptographically attested payload. The Tier E and Tier A proof format therefore carries no envelope-level duplicates of its signed claims, and there is no envelope-versus-signed-body consistency check to perform: the only field a Verifier reads ahead of signature verification is the protected-header kid, which is the untrusted-until-verified enrollment-lookup selector. A forged kid fails verification because the key it selects will not validate the signature, so no separate envelope-body comparison is needed to defend against a substituted routing value.

The Verifier looks up the enrollment by kid, verifies the JWS signature with the enrolled key, and only then reads the authentic claim set (including jti, psea_counter, psea_payload_hash, and ueid) directly from the verified payload. There are no pre-signature lookup copies of these values to reconcile.

The legacy envelope-body mismatch codes TOKEN_ACTIONID_MISMATCH and TOKEN_COUNTER_MISMATCH do not apply to the compact-JWS format. Now that all four tiers carry a single authoritative JWS payload with no envelope-level duplicates, these codes are retained in the error-code registry () only for legacy compatibility with pre-JWS producers that carried a separate envelope copy of an identifier or counter alongside the signed body.

section.name: Wire Transport Bodies
section.t: The transport body posted to each endpoint depends on the tier:

ul.li: Tier E: posted to /verify. Body is { proof, actionPayload, integrityEvidence?, requestId?, signalReport?, proofId? }, where proof is the compact JWS (), actionPayload is the unsigned cleartext action bound by psea_payload_hash (see Section 4.9), and integrityEvidence is the optional AttestationBlock (Section 4.5).
Tier A: posted to /authorize. Identical body shape to Tier E, with an optional contextLock when the Relying Party supplies it.

Tier S: posted to /sessionBatch. Body is { "summaries": ["<compact JWS>", ...] }, where each entry is a SessionSummary compact JWS with typ = "psea-session+jwt" (see ), plus optional event timeline entries.

section.name: Verifier Acknowledgement (JWS)
section.t: On a successful Tier E or Tier A appraisal, the Verifier returns a signed Attestation Result as a JWS Compact Serialization object () — the acknowledgement, or ACK. Its protected header carries alg = "ES256", a kid selecting the Verifier's published acknowledgement-signing key, and typ = "psea-ack+jwt". The SDK pins the Verifier acknowledgement-signing key at build time and rejects an ACK whose signature does not verify against it.

The signed ACK applies only to Tiers E and A. The Tier P (/trustAttest) and Tier S (/sessionBatch) responses are not signed: they are plain JSON. Tier P and Tier S are device-to-server verification paths in which the server is the verifier of the Attester's signed evidence, not a signer of evidence returned to the Attester; there is therefore no signed acknowledgement back to the device for these tiers. A Tier P or Tier S producer MUST NOT require a signed acknowledgement and MUST treat the HTTP status code plus the plain-JSON body (including any registered error code from ) as the authoritative outcome.
The ACK payload carries JWT registered claims plus PSEA-private acknowledgement claims:

dl.dd: JWT registered claims (): acknowledgement identifier, issued-at (epoch seconds), and expiry (epoch seconds).
The Verifier's decision for the appraised proof.
Identifier of the proof this ACK acknowledges.
Identifier of the enrollment the proof was verified against.
The accepted monotonic counter value.
The Verifier-computed chainEntry () for this proof. The SDK persists it as the next proof's psea_chain_prev.
Boolean result of the fail-closed action-binding check ().
The deployment policy evaluation result for this action.
Acknowledgement format version.

section.name: AttestationBlock
section.t: The AttestationBlock conveys the platform-issued attestation token that the Verifier uses to appraise the Attester's hardware-bound key against the platform Endorsement (Android Key Attestation root, Apple App Attest root, etc.). The wire shape of the AttestationBlock is intentionally minimal:
Field semantics:

dl.dd: A short identifier naming the attestation provider. Initial registered values: PLAY_INTEGRITY, APP_ATTEST. Future values are added via the IANA-managed registry in .

The platform-issued attestation artifact. The encoding is platform-specific: PLAY_INTEGRITY tokens are JWS-encoded; APP_ATTEST tokens are CBOR-encoded. The Verifier MUST parse token according to provider; no PSEA-defined canonical encoding applies to the token field itself.

section.name: Verifier Appraisal
section.t: The Verifier appraises the AttestationBlock by:

ol.li: Looking up the platform Endorsement (root certificate, public key, or equivalent trust anchor) for the named provider.
Parsing the token per the provider-specific format and validating its chain or signature against the Endorsement.
Extracting per-provider properties (package name / bundle identifier, security level, attestation challenge value, etc.) and comparing them to the Verifier's Reference Values.

Returning a per-provider rejection code (INTEGRITY_VERIFICATION_FAILED, INTEGRITY_PROVIDER_UNSUPPORTED, INTEGRITY_PROVIDER_INSUFFICIENT, ATTESTATION_SECURITY_LEVEL_INSUFFICIENT; see ) on failure, or proceeding to subsequent appraisal steps on success.

section.t: The internal structure of the token, the chain validation rules for each provider, and the choice of Reference Values are out of scope of this document; they are defined by the platform vendor's attestation specification and by the deployment's policy respectively.

section.name: Human Presence via User-Verification-Gated Signature
section.t: PSEA establishes the human-presence requirement () through the signing operation itself rather than through a separate wire-level presence block. The Attester's hardware-bound signing key MUST be gated by a platform user-verification event such that the signing operation cannot complete without a successful, contemporaneous user-verification ceremony. The signed proof body is therefore implicit Evidence that a user-verification event occurred at the moment of signing; the signature itself is the presence commitment.

The user-verification mechanisms that gate the signing key — for example, a platform biometric subsystem (fingerprint or face match), a Secure Enclave PIN entry, a hardware-token PIN, a smartcard with PIN, a magnetic-stripe credential combined with a PIN, or any equivalent platform user-verification primitive — are out of scope of this specification. The specific per-authenticator mechanism is mechanism-agnostic; what is normative is that the signing operation cannot complete without a contemporaneous user-verification event and that the proof carries an explicit psea_uv claim asserting that fact ().

The Verifier MUST NOT infer presence silently from the bare existence of a hardware-bound signature. For Tier E and Tier A it MUST require the explicit psea_uv claim and, where the authenticator's attestation conveys a UV-enforcement property, cross-check the claim against that attested property (appraised through the AttestationBlock () and the deployment's Reference Values). The detailed normative rule, and the honest statement of where this is attested versus where it rests on a documented trust assumption, are given in .

This design uses a single, compact user-verification claim rather than a parallel wire-level presence block whose other fields would duplicate information already carried by the AttestationBlock for platforms that bundle user-verification into the attestation chain. The cryptographic anchor for "a human was present at the moment of signing" is the psea_uv claim covered by the proof signature plus the hardware-bound-key attestation against which it is cross-checked.

section.name: User-Verification Claim (psea_uv)
section.t: Every Tier E and Tier A proof MUST carry a signed psea_uv claim:

ul.li: psea_uv.verified — a boolean asserting that a contemporaneous user-verification event gated the signing operation that produced this proof.

psea_uv.method — a string identifying the user-verification method. The value space is an extensible enumeration; registered baseline values include "biometric", "pin", and "fido_uv". A Verifier MUST tolerate an unknown method value (treat it as an opaque label) rather than rejecting solely on the method string.

section.t: A Tier P PToken MUST NOT carry psea_uv; Tier P makes no human-presence claim (). The claim is part of the JWS payload and is therefore covered by the proof's ES256 signature, so it is tamper-evident: an intermediary cannot flip verified from false to true without invalidating the signature.

Normative Verifier rule (Tier E and Tier A): the Verifier MUST require psea_uv.verified == true and MUST reject with USER_VERIFICATION_REQUIRED () otherwise. The Verifier MUST NOT accept psea_uv as merely self-asserted by the producer: it MUST anchor the claim to the authenticator's attested UV-enforcement capability. This requirement is device-agnostic — any conforming authenticator emits psea_uv, and the Verifier cross-checks it against that authenticator's attested UV-enforcement. Where the attestation conveys a UV-enforcement property and the psea_uv claim contradicts it (for example, the claim asserts verified == true but the authenticator's attested key properties show the signing key is not user-auth-gated), the Verifier MUST reject with UV_CROSS_CHECK_MISMATCH ().

Examples of the per-authenticator cross-check (informative, NOT normative — the specific mechanism is out of scope): a phone with an attested UV-gated hardware key whose key attestation conveys an auth-enforced / user-authentication-required property; a smartcard that produces a PIN-verified assertion; a FIDO authenticator that sets the user-verified (UV) flag in signed authenticator data. In each case the conforming authenticator emits psea_uv and the Verifier cross-checks it against that authenticator's own attested UV-enforcement.

Verification depth (known limitation — stated honestly, not overclaimed): where the authenticator's platform attestation conveys UV-enforcement (for example, a hardware-key attestation carrying an auth-enforced field), the Verifier cross-checks psea_uv against it and the user-verification property is attested. Where the platform attestation CANNOT convey UV-enforcement, conformance currently rests on a documented trust assumption in the authenticator's user-verification enforcement; in that case the psea_uv claim is required and signed, but it is not independently attested. Authenticator-signed user-verification evidence — for example, a FIDO-style UV flag carried in signed authenticator data — is the path to full verifiability and is the RECOMMENDED direction for authenticators that can produce it. This document does NOT claim the property is fully solved on every platform; it normatively requires the claim and the cross-check, and documents the residual trust assumption where the attestation surface does not yet permit the cross-check.

section.name: userIdHash
section.t: The userIdHash field is an Attester-signed subject-binding commitment: the SHA-256 of an opaque, deployment-issued subject identifier, encoded as base64url without padding (see ). The field cryptographically attributes the action to a subject identifier for the audit trail.

A Verifier MUST NOT make an authorization decision based on the per-proof userIdHash field on Tier E or Tier A. Subject attribution is for ledger and audit purposes only. The cryptographic chain of authorization at the Verifier rests on the device-bound signature, the monotonic counter, and the presence Evidence (); the Attester's commitment to a subject identifier is an additional audit-trail property, not a security gate.

The per-proof userIdHash is distinct from the enrollment-bound userIdHash recorded at enrollment time (). The enrollment-bound value IS used for decision-bearing checks in Tier P (the /trustAttest endpoint compares the PToken's userIdHash against the enrollment's userIdHash) and in enrollment-time challenge matching. The per-proof signed value on the Tier E / Tier A body is a separate commitment whose role is solely audit-trail attribution.

section.name: deviceState
section.t: The deviceState field carries an opaque device-posture commitment from the Attester. Its contents and the Verifier's appraisal logic are out of scope of this document.

On the wire, deviceState is a JSON object (or its CBOR equivalent) whose internal structure is not constrained by this specification. The Verifier appraises the commitment as part of the deployment's policy evaluation; the wire surface visible to the Attester is binary -- the Verifier either accepts the commitment (the proof proceeds through subsequent appraisal steps) or rejects with POSTURE_REJECTED (see ). The appraisal mechanism the Verifier applies, the categorical properties the commitment may carry, and any operator-side controls over appraisal sensitivity are deployment-specific and outside the scope of this specification.

Implementations SHOULD sort field keys per so the signed canonical bytes are byte-stable across re-issuance of the same posture commitment. A future revision of this document MAY define a normative sealed commitment form; until such a revision is published, conforming implementations treat deviceState as an opaque deployment-specific object whose contents are out of scope.

section.name: Counter Model (Per-Risk-Level Monotonic)
section.t: An Attester maintains five independent monotonic counters, scoped per risk level: LOW, MEDIUM, HIGH, CRITICAL, and PASSIVE. The signed-body counter field carries the value of whichever counter corresponds to the action's risk level at sign time. The Verifier's COUNTER_REPLAY check () compares the submitted value against the stored last-counter value for the same risk level, not against a single global counter.

Rationale (cross-tier replay protection while preserving offline operation): a single global per-Attester counter would conflict with PSEA's offline-capable property. Tier P, Tier S, and Tier E can all sign proofs while disconnected from the Verifier; if their counter values were drawn from one shared sequence, a Tier-E proof signed offline with counter N+1 would conflict on submission with a Tier-A proof signed online (after the Tier-E proof was composed but before it was synced) using the same N+1. Per-risk-level counters let each tier progress independently of the others.

The cross-tier replay surface that a single counter would defend against (a captured Tier-X proof submitted as Tier-Y) is closed instead by the global action_id_index uniqueness check the Verifier MUST maintain (each actionId may finalize exactly once across all tiers) plus the cross-replay binding of (the signed tier + audience fields force tier-correctness independent of counter scope).

The risk-level → tier mapping is given in : LOW → P, MEDIUM → S, HIGH → E, CRITICAL → A. The PASSIVE counter is used by the Tier P signing flow and corresponds to background-attestation traffic; it is independent of the LOW counter even though both map to Tier P at the tier-negotiation level (the PASSIVE counter exists because the SDK reference implementation issues PTokens on its own cadence, not strictly bound to a host-initiated LOW-risk action).
The five-counter design is an intentional deviation from earlier PSEA revisions that described a single per-Attester counter. The deviation is documented openly here for cross-platform parity.

section.name: ChainEntry
section.t: The chainEntry is a deterministic hash-chain anchor that links each Tier E and Tier A proof to the prior proof from the same Attester. The Attester carries the prior proof's chainEntry inbound as the signed psea_chain_prev claim; the Verifier MUST compare that value against its stored prior chainEntry for the Attester, and recomputes this proof's chainEntry from the signed inputs for return in the acknowledgement ().

section.name: Formula (Length-Prefixed Concatenation)
section.t: For each Tier E or Tier A proof, the chainEntry is computed over a length-prefixed concatenation of the three input fields. Length-prefixing guarantees domain separation: for any two distinct tuples (actionId, counter, chainPrev) the encoded inputs are byte-distinct regardless of whether any field contains the legacy : delimiter, NUL bytes, or any other character. This is the standard cryptographic pattern for unambiguous hash-input encoding.
section.artwork:
encode(s) = u32_be(len(utf8(s))) || utf8(s)
input = encode(actionId) || encode(decimal(counter)) || encode(chainPrev)
chainEntry = lowercase_hex( SHA-256( input ) )
section.t: where u32_be(n) is the 4-byte big-endian unsigned-32-bit encoding of the integer n, utf8(s) is the UTF-8 byte sequence of the string s, decimal(counter) is the digit-only decimal representation of counter per (the byte length of any field encoded by encode in this revision fits comfortably in u32), and the output is the lowercase-hex representation of the SHA-256 digest .
